title: Getting to ‘No’ Faster
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Admired Leadership Field Note tackles the demoralizing experience of a team pouring effort into a project only to have a leader kill it in seconds at the finish line, and argues the remedy is shared responsibility rather than better leadership alone. While all leaders hold the decision rights to negate or reset finished work, good leaders rarely exercise them late, whereas “imperial” leaders have a history of razing nearly complete projects. The note insists teams share the blame: they are obligated to surface success criteria and check in early and often so a leader is never surprised by a finished product. Its practical core is a set of upfront and mid-course mechanisms—establishing “kill criteria” (deadlines, budget, resources, and quality thresholds) before starting, scheduling an explicit early draft-concept review to confirm the leader endorses the general approach, and building staged go/no-go checkpoints so concerns surface before effort is wasted. It even advises asking a hesitant leader directly for the “probability of a No.” The counterintuitive framing—that reaching “No” faster is a win because it protects the team’s time and energy—reverses the usual instinct to avoid rejection, and the note closes by turning the lens on late-intervening leaders themselves.
points: The reframe is that a fast “No” is a form of respect for a team’s finite time and energy: redirecting or killing work early is far preferable to negating it after the heavy lifting, so “getting to No faster” is a goal to pursue, not avoid.

Responsibility is explicitly two-sided—teams are obligated to seek the leader’s success criteria and check in early and often rather than blaming the leader who blows up a finished product they were never shown in progress.
The concrete mechanism is defining “kill criteria” up front—deadlines, budget expectations, resource commitments, and quality thresholds—collaboratively with the leader before the work begins.
Explicit checkpoints are the safeguard: a first draft-concept review to lock in the general approach, followed by staged go/no-go reviews so the leader can voice concerns before work goes too far.
The note advises calibrating check-in intensity to the specific leader’s history and, when reluctance is sensed, asking directly for the probability of a “No” so the team isn’t blindsided later.
quotes: There is nothing more frustrating or deflating than spending oodles of time and energy on a project or initiative only to have it negated in a few seconds by a leader who doesn’t agree.

All leaders have the decision rights to negate or reset a project after the work has been done. Good leaders rarely assert those rights, while more imperial leaders typically have a history of razing nearly completed projects.

Teams and team members have an obligation to seek the guidelines and criteria for success for any project and to check in early and often so as not to surprise a leader with a finished product that they decide at the last minute they can’t live with.
They collaborate with the leader to establish the kill criteria before initiating the work.
Having a leader redirect the work at an early stage is much preferable to having them negate the project when it nears its conclusion.
A “No” is hard enough for a team to hear, but it is excruciatingly painful when it comes at the end of considerable work.
